background_notes.fact: For a compact subset C of finite-dimensional Euclidean space ℝ^n, C is closed and there exists R>0 with C⊂(−R,R)^n, including when C is empty.

grounds.reason: n is a positive finite integer.
F001 supplies compact C; S002 chooses that witness.

background_notes.justification: The open boxes (−k,k)^n for positive integers k cover Euclidean space. A finite subcover of nonempty compact C is contained in the box with the largest selected radius; for empty C choose R=1. Compact subsets of a Hausdorff space are closed: for a point outside C, separate it from each point of C by disjoint neighborhoods, use a finite subcover on C and intersect the corresponding neighborhoods of the outside point. Thus the complement used in S003 is open.

background_notes.fact: For a positive finite real R and finite positive integer n, Q=[−R,R]^n is compact and Lebesgue measurable, int Q=(−R,R)^n, and its Lebesgue measure is (2R)^n<∞.

grounds.reason: S003 chooses this R and defines Q as the corresponding closed box.

background_notes.justification: Closed bounded intervals are compact and their finite product is compact. Interior in finite-dimensional Euclidean space is the product of the open interiors of these nondegenerate intervals. Lebesgue measure of a rectangle is the product of its side lengths, here n factors 2R, so the box has the stated finite measure.

background_notes.fact: On an open Euclidean domain a smooth map has smooth derivatives of every finite order. Finite dot products, sums and squares of these derivatives, and derivatives of these scalar products, are smooth. If the map is constant on an open subset, every positive-order derivative vanishes there. Consequently all fields listed in S003 are jointly continuous and vanish outside C at times in int J.

grounds.reason: u is jointly smooth on ℝ^n×(0,∞).
C is the chosen compact witness; BG001 makes its complement open.
J has strictly positive endpoints, so its interior lies in the smooth domain.
The scalar fields in question are the indicated finite expressions in derivatives of u.

background_notes.justification: Differentiation is local, so derivatives of a locally constant map equal those of the constant map and hence vanish; iteration gives every positive order. Derivatives of a smooth map are smooth, and the ordinary sum and product rules preserve smoothness for these finite polynomial expressions. Thus e is smooth and e_t is smooth. On the open constant region e and u_t·∂_{x_j}u are identically zero, so their indicated derivatives are zero there as well; the remaining products have zero derivative factors. Smoothness implies the required joint continuity.

background_notes.fact: A continuous real function f on ℝ^n which vanishes outside a subset C of a compact finite-measure box Q is bounded on Q, Lebesgue measurable and absolutely integrable, with ∫|f|≤M·measure(Q) for some finite M≥0.

grounds.reason: F003 gives joint continuity, vanishing off C and finite measure of Q with C⊂Q.
Q is the closed box, compact by BG002.
An arbitrary r∈int J is fixed and each listed real scalar field is restricted to that spatial section.

background_notes.justification: Restriction of a jointly continuous function to a fixed-time section is continuous, hence Borel and Lebesgue measurable. Its absolute value attains a finite maximum M on nonempty compact Q. Since f vanishes off C⊂Q, |f|≤M1_Q everywhere. The bound is integrable with integral M·measure(Q)<∞, so monotonicity of the nonnegative Lebesgue integral gives absolute integrability. Apply separately to each listed scalar field and each finite spatial index.
